planting.note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings or set out container plants in lean, fast-draining sandy soil in full sun along the coast; established plants shrug off salt spray and wind and need no irrigation once rooted in.

directions: This silvery, finely dissected subshrub forms rounded mounds along Monterey and Big Sur coastal bluffs, dunes, and the edges of Monterey pine and cypress groves, where its felted gray-white foliage reflects salt-laden wind and sun. Flattened clusters of small bright-yellow flowers open from late spring into summer above the foliage, drawing butterflies and other pollinators. It is one of the toughest shrubs for exposed, sandy, salt-sprayed sites and spreads naturally by layering where lower branches touch the ground. Cut back hard every few years to keep the loose, sprawling habit from becoming woody and open in the center.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or small container stock in fall into lean, fast-draining sandy or gravelly soil in full sun; withhold summer irrigation once established, since manzanitas are highly prone to root rot in wet or heavy soil.

directions: A low, mat-forming manzanita of sandy maritime chaparral around Monterey Bay, this species hugs the ground with small, rounded, glossy leaves on reddish, slowly spreading branches. Clusters of small white to pale-pink urn-shaped flowers open in winter, followed by small reddish-brown berry-like fruits that birds and small mammals feed on. Its dense, low habit makes it a durable evergreen groundcover for erosion control on dry coastal slopes where few other shrubs will knit the ground together. Give it excellent drainage and lean soil, and avoid summer water, overhead sprinklers, and disturbing the shallow root crown, which are the most common causes of decline in cultivated manzanitas.

planting.note: Nick or lightly sand the hard seed coat and direct sow in fall into loose, sandy soil in full sun so seedlings can take advantage of winter rains; this dune species resents transplanting once its deep taproot develops.

directions: This shrubby, silver-leaved lupine stabilizes coastal dunes from Monterey Bay south through Big Sur, forming rounded mounds of soft, silvery-haired palmate foliage that reflect intense sun and salt wind. Dense spikes of blue-violet, pea-shaped flowers open in spring and are heavily visited by bees and butterflies, and as a nitrogen-fixing legume it helps build fertility in the poor, shifting sand it grows in. It is naturally fast-growing but relatively short-lived, often declining after five to ten years, so letting a few seed pods mature and drop each season helps keep a planting self-renewing. Give it full sun and sharp drainage, and avoid summer water or rich soil, both of which shorten its lifespan and encourage fungal disease.

planting.note: Direct sow or set out small plugs in fall into sandy, fast-draining soil in full sun on open, exposed sites; this short-lived coastal bluff species self-sows readily where the soil stays lean and uncrowded.

directions: Growing wild on coastal bluffs, dunes, and grassy headlands from Sonoma County south to Monterey, this wallflower forms a low rosette of narrow, grayish-green leaves topped by rounded clusters of pale yellow to cream flowers from late winter into spring. It is listed by the California Native Plant Society as a plant of limited distribution worth watching, though it remains available through specialty native-plant nurseries and is not under formal legal protection. Plants are typically short-lived, persisting a few years before dying back, but they reseed freely in open, disturbed, sandy ground to keep a patch going. Grow it in lean, well-drained soil in full coastal sun and avoid heavy mulch or rich fertilizer, which favor weeds over this plant's naturally sparse habitat.
sources: California Native Plant Society Rare Plant Program
